title: Variability in automated sepsis case detection: a systematic analysis of implementation methods in clinical data repositories.
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
desc: [Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA] To systematically review and characterize methodological heterogeneity in sepsis case detection using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care III (MIMIC-III) and eICU-CRD databases. We conducted a PRISMA-guided systematic review of PubMed and Web of Science (publication years 2016-2024). Studies were eligible if they applied the SOFA-based Sepsis-3 definition to MIMIC-III or eICU-CRD, provided at least one explicit label-calculation detail, reported a traceable detection rate, and met further criteria detailed in the PRISMA flow diagram. We classified each study by study type and unit of analysis (patients, admissions, or ICU stays) and extracted methodological details on sepsis case detection across 6 domains. For studies with available source code, we additionally examined code structure and repository dependencies to identify methodological decisions across these domains. Of 396 publications screened, 64 met inclusion criteria and 12 provided source code. Sepsis detection rates ranged from 3.4% to 65.2% in MIMIC-III and from 9.8% to 47.9% in eICU-CRD. Substantial variability persisted among studies using identical cohort definitions within both databases (MIMIC-III: 16.9%-42.2%; eICU-CRD: 13.9%-31.4%). In a generalized linear mixed model, between-study heterogeneity was extreme (overall τ²≈0.79; 95% prediction interval for a new study's detection rate 5%-63%), and study-level characteristics-including database, study type, infection detection method, code availability, and unit of analysis-explained only a small proportion of this variance (≈9%), with no characteristic reaching statistical significance. The overall proportion of studies reporting methodological details varied by domain: SOFA calculation (53.1%), infection detection methods (42.2%), temporal windows (37.5%), aggregation methods (26.6%), and missing-data handling (17.2%). Source code analysis identified 321 implementation decisions, revealing heterogeneity in baseline SOFA definitions (SOFA = 0 vs dynamic baseline), temporal windows (infection-centered vs ICU-admission-centered) and infection detection methods (antibiotic-culture matching vs APACHE-based diagnosis). Dependencies among several MIMIC-III repositories suggested propagation of implementation decisions across studies. Clinically validated sepsis definitions yield substantially different detection rates across studies using identical datasets. title: Feasibility of Real-Time Integration of a Large Language Model in the EHR to Identify Goals-of-Care Documentation.
source: PubMed · Journal of pain and symptom management
desc: [Journal of pain and symptom management] This article describes integration of a large language model (LLM) into the electronic health record (EHR) to identify unstructured goals-of-care (GOC) documentation or discrete data entry. To determine whether a prompt-engineered LLM reliably detects GOC documentation in clinical notes comparable to human experts and can display this evaluation to clinicians in real time. An interdisciplinary team of palliative care experts created an adjudicated reference standard, which was used to evaluate LLM models in detecting GOC documentation. Given this, the best-fit model (GPT-4o) was then integrated with the EHR for a six-month pilot at four hospitals, then released enterprise-wide. GPT-4o achieved the best performance (specificity 0.95, recall 0.74, precision 0.78). Manual audit on AI-flagged notes (n=325) confirmed substantial expert agreement (86%). In subgroup analyses, there was no statistically significant differences across race, sex, or age (specificity range 0.91-1; all p-values > 0.05). At enterprise scale, the model identified 37,000 patients with GOC documentation within approximately two months. In comparison to those without, patients with AI-flagged GOC documentation had higher acuity rates (ICU stay ≥5 days: 30.2% vs 8.2%; in-hospital mortality: 14.9% vs 0.6%; hospice discharge: 10.5% vs 0.4%). Code status changes were also significantly more frequent (29.3% vs 9.9%; p<0.05). Our initiative met the original objectives by providing a financially sustainable EHR optimization that converts unstructured, high-value GOC narratives into real-time discoverable and trackable documentation. Detecting and displaying these conversations is crucial, increasing clinical situational awareness while reducing documentation burden, leading to enhanced goal-concordant care.

title: Safety, Feasibility, and Acceptability of the MINERVA Voice Conversational Agent for Emergency Department History-Taking
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center; conditions: History Taking, Artificial Intelligence (AI); type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 250; status: ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION] This study evaluates whether an artificial intelligence (AI) conversational agent called MINERVA (Medical Interface for Navigating the Emergency Room with Voice Assistance) can safely and feasibly gather medical histories from emergency department (ED) patients and produce accurate summaries. The main questions it aims to answer are: Can an AI conversational agent gather and summarize patient histories in the emergency department? Are the resulting summaries accurate? Do they capture essential clinical information? Can an AI agent overseeing these conversations independently identify red-flag symptoms that may need time-sensitive clinical interventions? Adult ED patients interact with MINERVA via either voice chat or typing on a keyboard. MINERVA asks them questions about their symptoms and generates a summary which the patients review for accuracy. MINERVA reviews the conversation for clinical red flags that suggest urgent evaluation is required. Participants fill out a survey providing feedback on their experience. The summary is not saved in the medical record and clinical care is not affected. Physician reviewers will evaluate the safety, accuracy, and clinical value of the MINERVA interview transcripts and summaries using standardized rubrics, including whether MINERVA was correct in identifying red-flag symptoms that may need time-sensitive clinical interventions.

title: Design and Technical Evaluation of a Standards-Based System That Delivers Enclave-Derived Case-Finding Models to Patients and Clinicians
desc: BackgroundResearch data enclaves such as the All of Us Research Program do not allow participant-level data, or models fitted to them, to leave, which makes it hard to deliver case-finding models, which flag patients with possibly uncoded conditions for clinician review, to patients and clinicians. ObjectivesWe describe and technically evaluate a system that fits models outside an enclave from released summary counts and delivers them through standard health information technology interfaces. MethodsWe exported dissemination-compliant summary counts from the All of Us Researcher Workbench and, outside the enclave, fitted versioned models for Long COVID, chronic fatigue, fibromyalgia, endometriosis, Lyme disease, lupus, migraine, depression, and anxiety. A model contract (a model file and a written specification), a Python reference implementation, and synthetic Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) test patients define the expected outputs. One JavaScript scorer runs in a patient demonstration, a SMART on FHIR clinician application, and a CDS Hooks service. An atlas displays aggregate results. We evaluated the system on synthetic records with automated tests, cross-implementation output comparison, launches through the public SMART sandbox, and a counterexample review of the scoring and display rules. ResultsThe deployed Long COVID model had an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.67 in a random validation split. The eight self-report models reached 0.61 to 0.82 in identifying self-reporters without a code. The JavaScript scorer reproduced all 162 reference outputs exactly, and all 437 automated tests passed. A counterexample review found 5 classes of failure, including scoring ineligible patients and treating unavailable data as absent, all fixed and added as tests. ConclusionsModels fitted from released summary counts can be delivered through FHIR, SMART on FHIR, and CDS Hooks with reproducible scoring on synthetic records. Real-record interoperability, usability, and prospective clinical performance remain to be evaluated.

title: Targeting PRMT5 Across Cancers and AI-Driven Discovery of Candidate Compounds
desc: Protein arginine methyltransferase 5 (PRMT5) is a promising anticancer target, yet existing inhibitors shown limited clinical efficacy. Here, we paired multi-omics pan-cancer profiling with a machine learning virtual screening pipeline. Bioinformatics analyses with TIMER3, GEPIA2, UALCAN/CPTAC, the Human Protein Atlas, cBioPortal, STRING and Enrichr revealed widespread of PRMT5 mRNA expression, protein abundance, survival, genetic alteration, immune infiltration and co-expression networks with tumor-specific prognostic impact in GBM, LGG and KIRC. A deep neural network screened about 1.5 million PubChem compounds and deep neural network reached a ROC-AUC = 0.9857 and prioritized three candidates, CID 44345182, CID 2794188 and CID 44345334. Subsequent molecular docking against PRMT5 (PDB ID: 4X61), ADMET filtering and toxicity prediction, and 100 ns molecular dynamics (MD) simulations identified CID 44345182 as the potential hit, similar the docking scores of -9.8 compared with -9.2 kcal/mol for the reference ligand in binding affinity and trajectory stability. These findings clarify the context-dependent roles of PRMT5 and further experiment validations are needed to establish CID 44345182 as a promising candidate.

title: Harnessing Artificial Intelligence to Predict Dental Crowding in Modern Orthodontic Practice: A Comprehensive Review.
source: PubMed · The Kaohsiung journal of medical sciences
desc: [The Kaohsiung journal of medical sciences] Dental crowding is fundamental to orthodontic diagnosis and treatment planning, yet what constitutes "crowding" remains surprisingly heterogeneous. Space analysis quantifies tooth size-arch length discrepancy, irregularity indices characterize alignment displacement, and clinician-assigned severity reflects broader diagnostic interpretation. This narrative review examines the evolution of crowding assessment from conventional space analysis and digital measurement to two-dimensional artificial intelligence (AI), three-dimensional point-cloud learning, and clinician-aware agentic AI. Digitalization improves efficiency and reproducibility but does not resolve fundamental dependencies on how crowding is defined, anatomically represented, and established as a reference standard. Two-dimensional models enable prediction from readily available images but are constrained by projection and scale, whereas three-dimensional approaches directly learn from dental surface representations and can capture local geometric relationships. In a companion study of 495 arches from 284 patients, PointNet++ achieved an R2 of 0.718 and a mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.54 mm for prediction of crowding. In a separate retrospective demonstration, a bounded Gemini-based Agent incorporating matched record-derived verbal information reduced MAE from 1.951 to 1.437 mm, whereas mismatched information degraded performance. These findings also illustrate that the target construct-the specific clinical feature of crowding that a model is trained to predict-may differ across assessment methods. Together, these findings highlight a fundamental challenge: improving prediction does not resolve ambiguity in the target construct. Future crowding AI should therefore align the target construct, reference standard, and input representation; preserve provenance and uncertainty; integrate complementary clinical information transparently; and route uncertain cases for expert review.

title: CT Radiomics and Deep Learning-Based Non-Invasive Model for Tracing Primary Sites of Adenocarcinoma Liver Metastases: Automatic Differentiation of Multiple Primary Digestive Tumors
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: West China Hospital; conditions: Liver Metastases, Gastric Adenocarcinoma, Colorectal Adenocarcinoma, Biliary Tract Adenocarcinoma, Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 700; status: COMPLETED] This is a retrospective observational study. Liver metastasis occurs frequently in digestive-system cancers. Identification of the primary tumor source of liver metastasis may pose clinical challenges. Biopsy is an invasive procedure associated with potential sampling errors. This study aims to develop and validate a non-invasive artificial-intelligence model based on contrast-enhanced CT images. The model integrates CT radiomics and deep learning to automatically determine the primary origin of adenocarcinoma liver metastases, including gastric adenocarcinoma, colorectal adenocarcinoma, biliary/gallbladder adenocarcinoma, and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. The investigators will retrieve historical medical records and de-identified abdominal contrast-enhanced CT images from patients diagnosed at West China Hospital, Sichuan University between January 2015 and August 2026. No new intervention or treatment will be administered to participants in this study.

title: Long COVID undercoding and prediction from releasable electronic health record summaries in All of Us
desc: ObjectiveTo estimate Long COVID undercoding in electronic health records (EHRs) against federal survey prevalence, and to evaluate a predictor of later coding that anyone can rebuild from counts a research enclave releases. Materials and MethodsAmong 23,790 All of Us adults with COVID-19, we compared coded shares with Household Pulse Survey prevalence. Among 23,300 adults uncoded at day 90, we predicted a first U09.9 code by day 455. We fitted naive Bayes and linear discriminant models outside the enclave from released counts and compared them with an elastic net fitted inside to the same patients and features. Tests were a random 20% of patients (4,680, 50 coded) and 18 held-out EHR sites (5,760, 60 coded). ResultsUnder survey-comparability assumptions, about 1 in 9 adults who ever had Long COVID carried its code, and the women-to-men coding ratio was 0.79 (95% sensitivity interval, 0.65-0.95). The released models areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) were 0.68 (95% CI, 0.60-0.75) on the patient test and 0.64 (0.55-0.72) at held-out sites, 0.049 (0.001-0.104) above the elastic net. On the patient test, the elastic net had a higher area under the precision-recall curve (difference 0.062, 0.003-0.122). Released probabilities overestimated coding risk at held-out sites. DiscussionFitting from released counts did not consistently lower discrimination. Coded outcomes inform disease discrimination only under stated coding assumptions. ConclusionLong COVID is substantially and unevenly undercoded, and a model rebuilt from public counts predicts its later coding with moderate discrimination.

title: Automated screening of privacy risks in medical AI
desc: Medical artificial intelligence (AI) models are often shared without their training data, assuming this protects the patients who contributed them. However, a model can reveal whether a patient's records were used in training, a privacy breach known as a membership inference attack. This risk is usually reported as a cohort average, which can appear negligible while individual patients are almost certainly exposed. Identifying potentially vulnerable records before developing a production model could make privacy assessment more practical. We measured each patient's vulnerability to membership inference attack, across 7,789 models trained on six clinical datasets in four modalities, including two adapted pretrained medical models. Training choices changed how many patients had high attack scores, but the patients who ranked highest by risk largely stayed the same across the configurations we tested. Stronger weight decay reduced the exposed cohort up to threefold, yet largely the same patients remained most at risk across training recipes, architectures and initializations, including foundation models. Therefore, we developed a lightweight screening tool that uses four small models to identify patients with high risk of exposure before production-model training. We also assessed if flagged patients could be protected without removing their data. Privacy screening should become incorporated into data preparation for clinical AI.

title: TiSAM: fusing spatial and histopathology foundation models for whole-slide image segmentation
desc: Semantic segmentation of whole-slide images (WSIs) quantifies tissue composition and architecture, but existing models require extensive annotation and lose accuracy as the number of tissue classes increases or on heterogeneous, cross-scanner datasets. Here, we present the Tissue Segment Anything Model (TiSAM), which fuses SAM3 spatial features with UNI2-h pathology features within a multi-scale decoder. Because public benchmarks contain few tissue classes, we release MegaMouse, comprising 36,833 annotations of 52 tissue classes from 12 mouse organs, and an 11-class human pancreas dataset. TiSAM achieved the highest overall performance across four public datasets compared to existing convolutional neural network and vision transformer models, maintained high accuracy on MegaMouse, and maintained high accuracy in the human pancreas dataset when trained on as few as 5 annotated WSIs where previous integrations of SAM with pathology foundation models did not. TiSAM segmentations were also more consistent across eight slide scanners compared to other models. These results establish TiSAM as a general and highly adaptable framework for tissue segmentation, enabling studies containing many tissue classes, limited annotations, or images from multiple scanners.

title: Artificial intelligence, explainable deep learning, and generative models for osteoporosis and bone disease prediction: a systematic review and future research roadmap.
desc: [Frontiers in artificial intelligence] Osteoporosis is a major global health burden, with considerable morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs. Artificial intelligence (AI) has opened new avenues for osteoporosis screening, bone mineral density quantification, fracture-risk prediction, and clinical decision support, but progress remains fragmented across machine learning, deep learning, explainable AI (XAI), generative models, and multimodal learning. This systematic review brings these strands together and identifies priority research needs for AI-based osteoporosis prediction. Following the PRISMA 2020 statement, studies were identified from Scopus and Google Scholar, published between January 2020 and the final search date of 30 June 2026, with two reviewers screening independently and resolving disagreements by consensus. Design-related risk-of-bias indicators, such as retrospective vs. prospective design, validation strategy, and reference standard, were recorded for every study; a full PROBAST, QUADAS-2, and Newcastle-Ottawa Scale appraisal is planned but not yet complete. Fifty-eight studies met the inclusion criteria and were synthesized narratively and descriptively, without formal meta-analysis, given substantial heterogeneity. Findings spanned five themes: classical machine learning, deep learning for imaging, explainable AI, generative models, and multimodal learning. Deep learning achieved strong predictive accuracy (AUC 0.82-0.96), XAI improved clinical interpretability, generative models helped offset data scarcity, and multimodal approaches boosted performance by combining imaging and clinical data. Key gaps remain, including limited external validation, heavy reliance on retrospective data, poor generalisability, and limited regulatory readiness. Building on these findings, this review proposes MXGNet, a multimodal, explainable, generative framework incorporating privacy-preserving federated learning, intended to guide development of robust, interpretable, clinically deployable AI tools for osteoporosis prediction.
